unit.title: Conduct research and prepare a marketing plan to achieve goals

summary: This unit teaches managers to research a market and prepare a marketing plan. You will learn to set SMART marketing objectives, plan and carry out research, analyse findings and the situation, segment and target the market, design the marketing mix and prices, set a budget and action plan, monitor with KPIs and meet legal and ethical standards.

blocks.p: This unit is part of the Business Administration (Management) Level 5 qualification. It is for managers who must find out what customers and the market want, and then write a **marketing plan** that helps the organisation reach its goals. A marketing plan is a written document that sets marketing objectives, says which customers will be served and how, sets the budget, assigns the actions and says how results will be measured. **Market research** is the planned collection and analysis of information to support those decisions.

A plan built on opinion is a gamble. A plan built on research is a decision. This kit follows the order of the work: link marketing objectives to the business plan, plan and carry out research, analyse the situation, segment and target the market, design the marketing mix, set the budget, plan the actions, monitor the results and meet legal and ethical standards.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means in your unit
rows: Turn business goals into SMART marketing objectives.
Write a research brief, choose primary and secondary methods, design a sample and a questionnaire and check data quality.
Work out percentages and market share, and use SWOT, PESTLE, competitor analysis and the product life cycle.
Divide the market, choose the target segments and decide how the brand will be seen.
Choose product, price, place and promotion, and for services people, process and physical evidence.
Set a budget linked to objectives, with a contingency, and plan actions with owners and dates.
Choose KPIs, compare results with targets and adjust.
Respect consumer protection, data protection and honest research and advertising.

ul: A multiple-choice theory paper with many short scenarios and sums.
A written paper with short answers (terms such as primary, secondary, sample, pilot, KPI, SMART, price skimming) and longer answers where you plan research, design a mix or justify a budget.
Group practical tasks: a small research project, and a one-year marketing plan presented to a management panel.

blocks.note: Many questions include a percentage, a market share, a cost per customer or a budget split. Work every sum twice and write the unit.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: From business goals to marketing objectives

blocks.p: A marketing plan serves the **business plan**. If the organisation wants to raise profit by 10%, marketing must say which sales, from which customers, by when, will help to deliver that. Objectives that are not drawn from the business plan may produce activity that does not help the firm.

head: Letter
Meaning
Check yourself
rows: What exactly will change, for which product and market?
Can we do it with our people, money and time?
Does it support the business goals?

head: Weak objective
SMART objective
rows: Raise sales of 1-litre bottles in Manchester and St Elizabeth by 15%, from J$20,000,000 to J$23,000,000, between January and December
Raise unprompted awareness of the brand among adults in Kingston and St Andrew from 18% to 28% by 31 December, measured by a survey
Win 300 new account customers by 30 June

ol: Executive summary: goals, actions and budget on one page (written last, placed first).
Situation analysis: market, customers, competitors, SWOT and PESTLE.
Marketing mix: the actions for each P.
Action plan and schedule, with owners.
Monitoring and control: KPIs and review dates.

blocks.note: Put the summary first because senior managers read it first. It should state the goals, the main actions and the budget.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Planning and carrying out market research

blocks.p: Before collecting any data, write down the **research problem** and the **questions to answer**. For example: "Why have sales of our product fallen in Montego Bay, and what will win customers back?" The brief also states the methods, sample, budget, timetable and who will do what. A clear brief stops a firm from collecting information it will never use.

head: Feature
Secondary research
Primary research
rows: New information collected first-hand for this purpose
Published statistics, trade reports, rivals' websites, the firm's sales records
Surveys, interviews, focus groups, observation, test sales
Quick and cheap; may cover the whole market and several years
Fits the question exactly; up to date; owned by the firm
Collected for another purpose; may be out of date
Slower and costlier; needs good design
Starting out, sizing the market, spotting trends
The facts needed do not yet exist anywhere

blocks.p: A sensible order is **secondary first, then primary** to fill the gaps.

head: Type
What it gives
Methods
Strength
rows: Reasons, feelings and ideas in words
In-depth interviews, focus groups (a small discussion group led by a moderator), observation
Explains why people act as they do
Numbers that can be counted and compared
Surveys with many respondents, sales data, test sales
Measures how many, how much, and allows comparison

blocks.p: Use qualitative research to explore, then quantitative research to measure. A hotel that wants to understand, in depth, how guests feel about its spa should interview a small group of guests. A firm that wants to know what share of customers would pay J$500 for a product needs a survey.

ul: **Observation:** counting customers, watching how they move through a shop.
**Mystery shopping:** trained shoppers test service and prices lawfully, in the open market.
**Test marketing:** selling in a small area first to learn before a full launch.
**Web and social media data:** visits, enquiries, comments (public data, handled in line with the data protection law).

flow: Write the research problem and questions
Decide the primary method, the sample and the budget
Design and pilot-test the questionnaire or guide
Check, analyse and interpret the findings
Report with recommendations and use them in the plan

sections.title: Samples, questionnaires, data quality and analysing findings

blocks.p: A **population** is everyone you want to learn about. A **sample** is the smaller group chosen to represent it. A sample that is chosen well can describe a large population. A poor sample misleads, however many people it contains.

head: Method
How it works
Comment
rows: Every member of the list has an equal chance, for example picked by random numbers
Fair, if the list is complete
Divide the list into groups (strata) and sample from each in proportion
Makes sure each group is represented
Interviewers must find set numbers of each type of person
Common in street and mall surveys; not random
Ask whoever is easy to reach
Cheap, but may not represent the market

blocks.p: Worked example: a firm has 2,000 hotel accounts and 400 household accounts and can survey 240. It wants both groups represented. A 10% sample from each group: hotels 200, households 40, total 240.

ul: One idea in each question; plain, everyday words.
No **leading** questions that push towards an answer ("Don't you agree our coffee is the best?").
No **loaded** wording, and no questions that mix two ideas.
Answer choices that cover all possibilities, with "other" where needed.
Start with easy questions; leave personal questions to the end.
Keep it short; say how long it will take.
**Pilot-test** with a few people to find unclear questions before the main survey.

head: Check
Why it matters
rows: Is the sample representative of the target market?
If most replies come from people who recently complained, the results do not represent all customers
Too small a sample gives unreliable results
A very low rate raises the risk that those who replied differ from those who did not
Is the information current and from a reliable source?
Old or doubtful figures lead to poor decisions
Are the results reported honestly, including limits?
Shaping results to please the boss wastes the research

blocks.p: Check each sum a second way (for example, 15% of 600,000,000 is 90,000,000). Then **use the finding**: for example, if 40% of customers find the website hard to use, set an objective and actions to fix it.

sections.title: Situation analysis: the market, competitors and the environment

blocks.p: The test: strengths and weaknesses are **internal** and can be changed by the firm; opportunities and threats are **external** and must be responded to. Use SWOT to set priorities: use strengths to take opportunities, fix weaknesses that expose the firm to threats.

head: Factor
Examples a Jamaican marketer may track
rows: Government policy, trade agreements, public-sector buying rules
Inflation, exchange rates, incomes, interest rates, fuel and transport costs
Population, age mix, lifestyles, health awareness, migration
Smartphone use, online payment, social media, new equipment
Consumer protection, labelling, data protection, employment law
Hurricanes, drought, waste rules, customers' green preferences

blocks.p: Place each item under one heading, then note what it means for the plan. Rising fuel prices that raise delivery costs are **economic**. A new labelling rule is **legal**. A shift to ordering by phone apps is **technological**.

ul: Who are the direct rivals (same product) and indirect rivals (different products meeting the same need)?
What are their prices, range, locations, promotions, strengths and weaknesses, and target customers?
What are they likely to do next?

blocks.p: Use **lawful sources**: published price lists, websites, advertisements, trade shows, mystery shopping, customers' comments and public reports. Do not obtain a rival's confidential information.

head: Stage
Typical features
Marketing response
rows: Low sales, high costs, few rivals
Cut costs, harvest or withdraw; consider renewal

blocks.p: No firm can serve everybody equally well. **STP** is the sequence: segment the market, target the best segments and position the brand.
**Market segmentation** divides a market into groups with similar needs. Common bases:

head: Basis
Examples
rows: Parish, urban or rural, near a highway
Age, income, gender, family size, occupation
Lifestyle, values, interests (a gym grouping people by lifestyle)
How often they buy, loyalty, benefits sought, usage

blocks.p: Choose segments that are **big enough, growing, reachable, matched to the firm's strengths and where rivals are weaker**. A growing segment that the firm can serve better than rivals is more attractive than a larger one where rivals dominate. Work out the revenue potential: if a segment has 800 people, the firm expects to win 15% and each pays J$38,000, then 120 customers bring J$4,560,000.
**Positioning** is how customers see the brand compared with rivals. Choose a clear, believable position, write it as a statement and make the whole mix support it.

head: Part of the statement
Example
rows: Evening skills they can use at once
Short evening courses with job-placement help
Day colleges that need a full-time commitment

blocks.note: A position must be true. If research shows customers do not see you as you intend, change the activity or the claim, not the research.
blocks.label: Remember

head: P
Decisions for the manager
rows: Features, quality, range, brand, packaging, service
Price level, discounts, credit terms, price to the customer including GCT at the current rate
Where and how customers buy: shops, agents, online shop, delivery, location
Advertising, personal selling, sales promotion, public relations, social media, word of mouth
How the service is delivered: booking, waiting, handling complaints
What customers can see: premises, uniforms, certificates, website, documents

blocks.p: The mix should fit the **target segment and the positioning**. A courier with complaints about late and lost parcels should fix **process** first. A clinic that wants to be seen as professional must check its **physical evidence**: clean rooms, visible qualifications and tidy documents.

head: Strategy
What it is
When it suits
rows: Cost plus a percentage on cost
Simple; check that the market will accept it
A low price to win many customers quickly, with plans to raise it later
New firms seeking share; price-sensitive markets
A high launch price to early buyers, lowered later
Distinctive new products with keen early buyers
Similar products in a crowded market
Price by what the customer believes it is worth

blocks.p: Worked example, mark-up: a product costs J$360 to make and sell. A mark-up of 50% on cost adds J$180, so the price is J$540 before GCT. (Mark-up is a percentage of **cost**; margin is a percentage of the **selling price**: 180 ÷ 540 = 33.3% margin.) Allow for GCT at the current rate when setting a price to the public, and say whether a quoted price includes it.

Worked example, break-even: fixed costs of J$600,000 a month, price J$540, variable cost J$360 per unit. Each unit contributes J$540 − J$360 = J$180. Break-even = 600,000 ÷ 180 = 3,333.3, so the firm needs **3,334 units** a month to cover its costs.

ul: Choose channels that reach the target segment at reasonable cost: a craft producer seeking overseas buyers may use its own online shop with courier delivery.

Business buyers of equipment often trust **personal selling** by trained account staff. Public buyers respond to advertising on the channels they use: if young customers learn about products mainly through short phone videos, move that segment's spending there.
Likes are not sales: if posts are liked but do not sell, check whether they reach and persuade the target buyers.
Combine methods so that they repeat one message.

sections.title: Budget, action plan, monitoring and control

head: Method
How it works
Comment
rows: A set percentage of expected sales (5% of J$48,000,000 is J$2,400,000)
Simple, but spending follows sales, not goals
What is left after other costs
Cost the tasks needed to reach each objective and add them up
Links spending directly to goals; preferred

blocks.p: Worked example: a firm with J$3,300,000 allocates: digital advertising and content J$1,320,000 (40%); in-store sampling J$825,000 (25%); radio J$660,000 (20%); print and point-of-sale J$330,000 (10%); contingency J$165,000 (5%). Total: 1,320,000 + 825,000 + 660,000 + 330,000 + 165,000 = J$3,300,000 and 100%. The **contingency** covers unexpected costs and chances.

head: Action
Owner
Start
Finish
Budget (J$)
KPI
rows: Samples given; sales in those shops

blocks.p: A **Gantt chart** shows each activity as a bar on a timeline, so the schedule and overlaps can be seen. Every action has a **named owner** so that someone is accountable.

A **key performance indicator (KPI)** is a measurable value used to track progress towards a goal. Choose KPIs that fit each objective. For "win 300 new account customers by June", the KPI is **new accounts opened each month**.

head: KPI
Working
Example
rows: Cost per new customer (or per enquiry)
Extra gross profit J$800,000 on a J$500,000 campaign: 300,000 ÷ 500,000 = 60%

flow: Set targets and dates for each KPI
Collect the figures each month (sales, enquiries, web visits, satisfaction)
Compare actual with target and note the gap
Adjust the actions or the budget; report to senior managers
Review the whole plan at set dates and at year end

blocks.note: If sales are 20% behind target halfway through the year, **find out why first**. The cause may be a late campaign, a stock problem, a rival's move or a poor target. The right response depends on the cause.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Law, ethics, consultation and writing the plan

ul: Claims must be **true and capable of proof**. "100% natural" is misleading if the product contains added colouring. "Cheapest in Jamaica" needs evidence.
Prices must be clear, including any extra charges.
Comparative advertising must be fair and accurate.
Do not make health or safety claims you cannot support.
Follow rules on labelling and on advertising to children.
Tell people the **purpose** of the research and obtain their **consent**; allow them to stop at any time.
Children need a parent's or guardian's consent.

Collect only the **personal data** needed, for the stated purpose; keep it secure and do not use it for another purpose (for example, sending sales messages to survey respondents who did not agree). This follows the data protection law.
Report results honestly, including their limits.
Do not pretend that research is something else, and do not use research as a disguised sales approach.
Gather competitor information only from lawful public sources. Refuse confidential information offered by a rival's former employee.

blocks.p: Before finalising the plan, **consult sales, finance, operations and customer-service staff**: they know what is realistic and affordable, and they must carry out the actions. Then present the plan to senior management for approval, with the summary first.

ul: Lead with the executive summary; keep the plan short and clear.
Use tables for objectives, budget and actions.
Show the source of every key figure.
State risks and contingency plans.
Check every sum twice and keep the document consistent.

blocks.note: A plan nobody owns will not happen. Each action needs an owner, a date, a budget line and a KPI.
blocks.label: Tip

ul: draw marketing objectives from the business plan and write them in SMART form.
write a research brief and choose between primary, secondary, qualitative and quantitative methods.
design a fair sample and a good questionnaire, and pilot-test it.
work out response rate, percentages, market share, average and conversion rate.
judge data quality and avoid biased results.
use SWOT, PESTLE, competitor analysis and the product life cycle.
segment a market, choose target segments and write a positioning statement.
design a marketing mix, using the 7Ps for services.
set a price using mark-up, and use penetration or skimming strategies appropriately; allow for GCT at the current rate.
build a budget with the objective-and-task method and a contingency.
prepare an action plan with owners, dates and a Gantt chart.
choose KPIs, monitor them and respond to gaps.
meet consumer protection, data protection and ethical standards in research and advertising.
consult colleagues and present a plan clearly.

c1.title: Coffee cooperative in St Andrew
c1.text: A coffee cooperative in the Blue Mountains wants a marketing plan to grow sales of ground coffee to hotels and to households. It has a list of 2,000 hotel and restaurant accounts and 400 household customers, and can afford to survey 240 people. A first draft question reads: "Don't you agree our coffee is the best on the island?" The cooperative has emailed 1,500 customers and 210 have replied. The manager, Mrs Maxine Duncan, also has published tourism statistics and the cooperative's own sales records.

c2.title: Evening courses in Mandeville
c2.text: A vocational training centre in Mandeville plans evening short courses in office skills. Research shows 800 working adults in the town want evening courses. The centre expects to win 15% of them at a fee of J$38,000 each. Rivals are day colleges that need a full-time commitment, and one private tutor who offers weekend courses. The centre's strengths are experienced instructors and a link to local employers.

c3.title: A new physiotherapy clinic in Savanna-la-Mar
c3.text: A new physiotherapy clinic is opening in Savanna-la-Mar. Each session costs the clinic J$2,800 in staff, supplies and running costs. The owner, Dr Natalie Reid, plans to add a mark-up of 50% on cost. Patients say they dislike long waits and want to see that the clinic is professional. Doctors in the parish may refer patients. A rival clinic is a long drive away.

c4.title: A tour operator in Montego Bay
c4.text: A Montego Bay tour operator expects sales of J$55,000,000 next year and sets its marketing budget at 6% of expected sales. A J$1,200,000 online campaign produced 150 new bookings. The objective for the year is 800 bookings by the end of December. By December the operator had 640. The manager, Mr Trevor Ellis, has set aside 5% of the budget as a contingency. The tasks needed to reach the 800-booking objective have been costed at J$3,900,000.

c5.title: A school uniform maker in Spanish Town
c5.text: A school uniform maker in Spanish Town is preparing its marketing plan. Its strengths are skilled seamstresses and a good reputation. A large retailer is opening a school-wear shop nearby. Parents increasingly order school items from their phones. The firm plans to advertise that it is "the cheapest uniform maker in Jamaica", though it has not compared prices. It also holds phone numbers from a survey, which respondents gave for a prize draw, and the sales manager wants to text them about discounts.

questions.q: The cooperative wants views from both hotels and households in the 240 sample, in proportion. How many hotel accounts should be in the sample?
questions.why: The list has 2,400 accounts and the sample is 10%. Hotels: 10% of 2,000 = 200; households: 10% of 400 = 40; 200 + 40 = 240. This is a stratified sample.

questions.q: What is the response rate of the email survey?
questions.why: 210 ÷ 1,500 = 0.14, so 14%. A low response rate raises the risk that those who replied differ from those who did not.

questions.q: What is the main fault of the draft question "Don't you agree our coffee is the best on the island?"
o: It is too short to give the cooperative useful data
It asks about two different products in one question
It uses technical words that the customers may not know
It is a leading question that pushes towards one answer
questions.why: A leading question suggests the answer wanted. A good question is neutral, such as "How would you rate the quality of our coffee?" with a scale of answers.

questions.q: Mrs Duncan has tourism statistics and the cooperative's sales records. Why should she start with these?
o: They are primary research that fits her questions exactly
They are secondary sources: quick, cheap and good for trends
They are the only legal source of data about the market
They remove the need for any survey of the customers
questions.why: Existing information gives a fast, low-cost picture of the market and helps to decide what primary research is still needed. They rarely answer every question about the firm's own customers.

questions.q: What kind of segmentation is used when the centre looks at working adults who want evening study?
o: Geographic only, because they live in Mandeville
Demographic and behavioural: job and benefit sought
Psychographic only, because they want to study
No segmentation, because the centre will serve everyone
questions.why: Working adults is a demographic group, and wanting evening courses is a benefit sought, which is behavioural. The centre is dividing the market by who people are and what they need.

questions.q: What is the expected revenue if the centre wins 15% of the 800 adults at J$38,000 each?
questions.why: 15% of 800 = 120 students. 120 × J$38,000 = J$4,560,000. J$30,400,000 is the fee times all 800 people.

questions.q: Which positioning statement is best supported by the facts?
o: Short evening courses for working adults, with employer links
The cheapest courses in the parish for every kind of learner
A full-time college experience offered in the evening
The only centre in Jamaica with experienced instructors
questions.why: A position must be true and appeal to the target. The centre's strengths are its instructors and its employer links, and its rivals need a full-time commitment. The other statements are unsupported or not matched to the target.

questions.q: The private tutor offers weekend courses. What should the centre do about this rival?
o: Obtain its student list from a former client of the tutor
Ignore it, because a private tutor is too small to matter
Find out its prices and content from lawful public sources
Copy its course outline and set the same fee
questions.why: Competitor analysis uses lawful sources such as advertisements, public price lists and customers' comments. Using a rival's confidential list is unethical and may be unlawful. Ignoring a rival ignores part of the market.

questions.q: What price should Dr Reid charge per session before GCT, using a 50% mark-up on cost?
questions.why: Mark-up is on cost: 50% of J$2,800 = J$1,400. Price = J$2,800 + J$1,400 = J$4,200. GCT at the current rate is allowed for separately.

questions.q: Patients dislike long waits. Which element of the services marketing mix needs most attention?
o: Price: the fee charged for each single session
Process: the way booking and appointments are run
Place: the location of the clinic building
Promotion: the radio advertisements planned
questions.why: Waiting time is part of how the service is delivered, which is process. Better booking, staffing and scheduling remove waits.

questions.q: Patients want to see that the clinic is professional. Which action best supports this?
o: Offer a lower price during the first month
Put up posters about the opening of the clinic
Show certificates, keep rooms clean and use tidy documents
Send text messages about the clinic to every resident
questions.why: Physical evidence is what customers can see and use to judge quality, such as premises, uniforms, certificates and documents. Price and posters do not show professionalism by themselves.

questions.q: Doctors in the parish may refer patients. What is the best way to use this?
o: Meet the doctors, explain the service and make referral easy
Pay doctors for each patient sent, without telling patients
Say that doctors recommend the clinic before they agree
Wait for the doctors to find out about the clinic themselves
questions.why: Referrals build trust through people the patients already trust. The clinic should build relationships and make the process easy. Hidden payments or false claims are unethical and may be unlawful.

questions.q: The budget is 6% of expected sales, but the tasks needed to reach the objective are costed at J$3,900,000. What is the position, and what should Mr Ellis do?
o: J$3,300,000, so J$600,000 short; review the tasks or ask for more
J$3,300,000, so J$600,000 over; return the unused money to the owners
J$330,000, so J$3,570,000 short; cancel the whole online campaign
J$3,300,000, so the plan is affordable; carry on with it unchanged
questions.why: 6% of J$55,000,000 is J$3,300,000. Costed tasks of J$3,900,000 leave a gap of J$600,000. A manager reviews whether every task is needed, or presents the evidence for extra funds. The task-based figure shows what the objective really needs.

questions.q: What was the cost per new booking for the online campaign?
questions.why: J$1,200,000 ÷ 150 = J$8,000. Cost per new customer is the campaign cost divided by the number won.

questions.q: What percentage of the annual booking target was achieved?
questions.why: 640 ÷ 800 = 0.8, so 80%. The gap is 20%, or 160 bookings. Always compare actual with target.

questions.q: How large is the contingency?
questions.why: 5% of J$3,300,000 = J$165,000. A contingency covers unexpected costs and chances, so the plan does not fail when something changes.

questions.q: Parents increasingly order school items by phone. Under which PESTLE heading does this trend fall?
o: Political
Technological
Environmental
Legal
questions.why: Ordering by phone apps is a change in technology and its use. It is a factor outside the firm that the plan must respond to.

questions.q: The retailer opening a school-wear shop nearby is which part of a SWOT analysis?
o: A threat, because it is external and harmful
A weakness, because it affects the firm
An opportunity, because it brings more people to the area
A strength, because it shows demand for uniforms
questions.why: Opportunities and threats come from outside the firm. A nearby rival with greater buying power is a threat that the plan should respond to.

questions.q: The firm wants to advertise that it is "the cheapest uniform maker in Jamaica" without comparing prices. What is the main problem?
o: Advertising prices is not allowed in Jamaica at all
The claim is acceptable if parents are likely to like it
The claim would be acceptable if printed in small type
The claim may mislead buyers and break consumer law
questions.why: Advertising claims must be true and capable of proof. An unsupported "cheapest" claim may mislead parents, and the firm could face complaints or legal action.

questions.q: The sales manager wants to text discounts to survey respondents who gave their numbers for a prize draw. What should the firm do?
o: Text everyone, because the firm already holds the numbers
Pass the numbers to the retailer next door for a fee
Use the numbers only for the stated purpose unless people agree
Delete the survey answers but keep the numbers for texting
questions.why: Personal data should be used only for the purpose stated when collected, and kept secure, in line with the data protection law. Texting offers needs consent.
